intro: About 1,100 years ago, a doctor in Baghdad noticed that two rashes were really two different diseases. A few hundred years later, a teacher in Italy held a human jawbone and saw that a famous book was wrong. In this unit, you will follow doctors who looked closely and asked, "Is that really true?"

You will visit great hospitals in Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo that cared for anyone who was sick. You will meet Ibn Sina, whose Canon of Medicine was taught for centuries, and see how books moved from Arabic into Latin. You will learn how Europe faced the Black Death, and how Vesalius, Harvey, Paré and Leeuwenhoek changed medicine by testing old ideas.

By the end, you will be able to explain how medical knowledge was built and shared across many cultures. You will also be able to tell the difference between trusting an authority and checking the evidence yourself.
bigQuestion: How did doctors across many cultures build medical knowledge, and when did seeing for yourself begin to matter more than old books?

title: From the Islamic Golden Age to the Renaissance

chapters.title: Hospitals and the Canon
chapters.bigQuestion: How did doctors in the Islamic world build knowledge that the whole world later used?

story.title: Two Rashes, One Careful Doctor
story.kicker: In Baghdad, a doctor refuses to call two sicknesses the same thing just because they look alike.
paragraphs: Baghdad, about 1,100 years ago. The city is one of the largest in the world. Ships and camel trains bring spices, paper and books. In a busy hospital, a doctor named Abu Bakr al-Razi walks between rows of beds. Many children lie there with fever and red spots on their skin.

Most people call every fever with spots by one name. Al-Razi is not sure they are right. He looks closely at each child. He writes down when the fever started, how the spots look, and where they spread. He asks the families questions. Day after day, his notes grow.

Slowly, a pattern appears. Some children have a high fever and back pain before bumps rise on the skin. The bumps fill up and can leave scars. Other children have red eyes, a runny nose and a cough, and their spots are flatter. Al-Razi decides these are two different diseases. Today we call them smallpox and measles.

Al-Razi writes a short book about the two sicknesses. He explains how to tell them apart and how to care for patients. Centuries later, the book is translated into Latin and other languages. His careful notes show a simple idea that still guides medicine: look closely, write it down, and compare.
story.think: Why does it matter to a patient whether a doctor can tell two look-alike sicknesses apart?

lessons.title: The Bimaristan
lessons.mainIdea: Cities in the Islamic world built large hospitals, called bimaristans, that cared for rich and poor alike.
reading: Picture a large building with courtyards, fountains and separate halls. Some halls are for fevers, some for eye problems, some for broken bones. A pharmacy mixes medicines. Doctors teach students at the bedside. This was a *bimaristan*, a hospital in the medieval Islamic world.

The word bimaristan comes from Persian and means "place of the sick." Rulers and wealthy families paid for these hospitals through gifts called *waqf*. A waqf was money or property given forever for a good cause. The income paid for doctors, food, beds and medicine.

Big cities such as Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo had bimaristans. Care was usually free. Men and women, locals and travelers, and people of different faiths could be treated. The goal was to care for anyone who was sick, not only those who could pay.

words.d: a hospital in the medieval Islamic world; the word means place of the sick
a gift of money or property set aside forever to pay for a good cause, such as a hospital

lessons.title: Great Hospitals of Three Cities
lessons.mainIdea: Famous hospitals in Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo became centers of care and teaching.
reading: In Baghdad, the capital of the Abbasid rulers, several hospitals were built in the 800s and 900s. Al-Razi worked in Baghdad. One story says he chose a spot for a new hospital by hanging pieces of meat around the city to see where they spoiled most slowly. Historians are not sure the story is true, but it shows how people remembered him as a doctor who tested things.

In Damascus, the ruler Nur al-Din founded a hospital in the 1150s. Part of its building still stands today. It trained doctors for many years. Students learned from books and from real patients in the wards.

In Cairo, the Sultan Qalawun opened the Mansuri hospital in 1284. It was huge. It had wards for different illnesses, a place for lectures and a large staff. Records describe music and storytelling to comfort patients. These hospitals show a *public health* idea: a city takes care of its sick people.

words.d: the work of keeping a whole community healthy, not just one person
a large room in a hospital for patients with a similar need

lessons.title: Al-Razi Tells Two Diseases Apart
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Razi used careful observation to show that smallpox and measles are different diseases.
reading: Abu Bakr al-Razi lived from about 865 to 925. In Europe he was later called Rhazes. He was born near modern Tehran in Iran and worked in Baghdad and in his home city of Rayy. He wrote many books on medicine, chemistry and ideas.

His most famous short book describes *smallpox* and *measles*. Before him, many writers mixed them up. Al-Razi listed the signs of each. Smallpox often began with high fever and back pain, and its bumps filled and scarred. Measles came with red eyes, a cough and flatter spots.

Telling diseases apart is called *diagnosis*. It matters because different diseases can need different care. Al-Razi also kept records of his patients. He believed a doctor should check old books against what patients actually showed. That habit is at the heart of medicine today.

words.d: a serious disease caused by a virus that made raised bumps on the skin; it was wiped out worldwide by 1980
a disease caused by a virus that brings fever, cough, red eyes and a flat red rash; a vaccine prevents it
figuring out which illness a person has from signs and tests

lessons.title: Ibn Sina Writes the Canon
lessons.mainIdea: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine, finished about 1025, gathered the medical knowledge of his time into one huge work.
reading: Ibn Sina lived from about 980 to 1037 in Central Asia and Persia. Europeans called him Avicenna. As a young man he read everything he could find. He was also a philosopher who wrote about logic and the mind.

His biggest medical book is *The Canon of Medicine*, finished about 1025. A *canon* is a set of rules or a standard collection. The Canon has five books. They cover how the body works, simple medicines, diseases of each part of the body, illnesses that affect the whole body, and mixed medicines.

Ibn Sina built on Greek writers such as Hippocrates and Galen. He also added his own observations. He wrote that some diseases can spread through water and soil, and that new medicines should be tested carefully. He still used the old Greek idea of four humors, which later science replaced.

words.d: a standard collection of rules or writings that people treat as the main guide
four body fluids that ancient Greek doctors believed controlled health; the idea was later replaced by science

look.title: What Is Medicine?
look.text: Medicine is the study of the human body in health and sickness, so that health can be kept and, when it is lost, brought back.
look.cite: Paraphrase of Ibn Sina, The Canon of Medicine, Book 1, about 1025
look.prompt: What two goals of medicine does Ibn Sina name here?

check.why: The reading dates the Canon to about 1025. 1543 is Vesalius's book.

check.q: Which old idea did Ibn Sina still use that science later replaced?

check.why: The reading says he used the Greek idea of four humors, later replaced.

check.q: What advice about new medicines appears in the reading?

lessons.title: A Textbook for Centuries
lessons.mainIdea: The Canon was used to teach doctors in Europe and Asia for several hundred years.
reading: Imagine a medical student in Italy around 1500. The main textbook on the desk is not by an Italian. It is a Latin version of Ibn Sina's Canon, written almost 500 years earlier and far away.

The Canon was clear and well organized, so teachers liked it. Universities in Europe used it into the 1600s. After printing began, it was printed many times in Latin. It was also studied across the Islamic world and in South Asia.

Using one book for so long had good and bad sides. Students shared a common *curriculum*, a set plan of study. But some teachers trusted the book more than their own eyes. As the next chapter shows, later doctors began to test the old books against real bodies.

words.d: the planned set of subjects and books that students study
a person or book that people trust and follow as the expert

look.title: Trust the Book or the Body?
look.text: A teacher reads aloud from the Canon about the liver. A student has just seen a liver during a lesson, and it does not match every line. The teacher says, "The book is older and wiser." The student is unsure.
look.prompt: What should the student do next, and why?

check.q: About how long did European universities use the Canon?

check.q: What is a curriculum?

check.why: The reading defines curriculum as a set plan of study.

check.q: What was a downside of using one book for so long?

check.why: The reading says some teachers trusted the book over what they saw.

lessons.title: Ibn al-Nafis and the Lungs
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1200s, Ibn al-Nafis correctly described blood passing from the heart through the lungs and back.
reading: Galen, a Greek doctor of the 100s CE, taught that blood seeped through tiny holes in the wall between the two sides of the heart. For about 1,000 years, most doctors agreed. The wall in the middle of the heart is called the *septum*.

Ibn al-Nafis, a doctor who worked in Damascus and Cairo, disagreed. In a commentary written in the 1200s, he said the septum is thick and has no holes. He reasoned that blood must travel from the right side of the heart to the lungs, mix with air there, and return to the left side.

This path is called the *pulmonary circulation*. Pulmonary means having to do with the lungs. Ibn al-Nafis was right. But his idea was not widely known in Europe. European doctors described the same path in the 1500s, and historians still discuss whether any of them had heard of his work.

words.d: the wall of muscle that divides the right and left sides of the heart
the path of blood from the heart to the lungs and back to the heart

look.title: Two Maps of the Heart
look.text: Map A (Galen): blood drips from the right side of the heart to the left through tiny holes in the middle wall. Map B (Ibn al-Nafis): the middle wall is solid, so blood leaves the right side, goes through the lungs, and comes back to the left side.
look.prompt: What would a doctor need to see inside a heart to decide which map is right?

check.why: The reading says he wrote that the septum is thick with no holes.

check.q: What does pulmonary mean?

check.q: Whose older idea did Ibn al-Nafis challenge?

lessons.title: From Arabic to Latin
lessons.mainIdea: Translators turned Arabic medical books into Latin, and this knowledge helped shape European medicine.
reading: In the 1100s, the city of Toledo in Spain held libraries full of Arabic books. Scholars came from across Europe to read them. One of them, Gerard of Cremona, spent years there. He is credited with translating dozens of works into Latin, including Ibn Sina's Canon.

Latin was the shared language of learning in Europe. A *translation* moves a text from one language into another. Earlier, in southern Italy, a scholar named Constantine the African had also translated Arabic medical books near the medical school of Salerno.

These translations carried Greek ideas that Arabic scholars had saved and added to, plus new Arabic work. Words also traveled. Alcohol and syrup, for example, come into English from Arabic. Knowledge moved from Greek to Arabic to Latin, and each step added something.

words.d: moving a text from one language into another
the language of the ancient Romans, used for learning across Europe for many centuries

look.title: A Chain of Languages
look.text: A Greek doctor writes about fevers. Centuries later, a scholar in Baghdad translates the book into Arabic and adds notes from his own patients. Later still, a scholar in Toledo turns the Arabic book into Latin. A student in Paris reads it.
look.prompt: At each step, what could be gained, and what could be lost?

check.why: The reading says Latin was the shared language of learning in Europe.

check.q: Which English word came from Arabic, according to the reading?
check.why: The reading names alcohol and syrup as words that came from Arabic.

lessons.title: Unani Medicine Today
lessons.mainIdea: Unani medicine, built on Greek and Arabic ideas, is still practiced today, especially in South Asia.
reading: In a clinic in Delhi or Hyderabad, a patient may visit a *hakim*, a practitioner of Unani medicine. The hakim asks about sleep, food and mood, and checks the pulse. The advice may include diet changes and herbal mixtures.

*Unani* comes from an Arabic word for Greek. Unani medicine holds that health depends on a balance of four humors and on a person's temperament. It grew from Greek writers, Ibn Sina and later scholars. In India, the government recognizes Unani as one of its traditional systems of medicine.

Scientists have tested some plants used in Unani, and a few show effects worth studying. For most Unani remedies, strong evidence from careful trials is still missing. Some herbal products can interact with other medicines. So anyone who uses them should tell their doctor or pharmacist.

words.d: a traditional medicine system based on Greek and Arabic ideas; the name comes from an Arabic word for Greek
a practitioner of Unani medicine
when one medicine or herb changes how another one works in the body

lessons.title: Care in the Monasteries
lessons.mainIdea: In medieval Europe, monasteries cared for the sick, grew healing plants and copied medical books.
reading: Picture a stone *monastery* in the countryside, around the year 1100. Monks tend a garden of sage, mint and other herbs. Inside, a room called the infirmary holds sick monks and travelers. Another room holds books that monks copy by hand.

A monastery is a community of monks or nuns who live by religious rules. The Rule of Saint Benedict, written in the 500s, told monks to give special care to the sick. Many monasteries became places of rest, food and nursing for people in need.

Hildegard of Bingen, a German abbess who lived from 1098 to 1179, wrote about plants and health. Monks and nuns saved old texts by copying them. Their care was kind and practical, though they did not know what caused most diseases.

words.d: a place where monks or nuns live, work and pray together by religious rules
a room or building for caring for sick people

look.title: The Rule on the Sick

lessons.title: The Black Death
lessons.mainIdea: The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 killed a large share of people in Europe and the Middle East, and it led to early quarantine rules.
reading: In 1347, ships reached Sicily carrying a deadly sickness. Within a few years it spread across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. People later called it the *Black Death*. Historians estimate it killed roughly one third to one half of Europe's people.

Today we know it was *plague*, caused by a bacterium carried by fleas on rats and other animals. People at the time did not know about germs. Many blamed bad air or the stars. Some cruelly blamed Jewish communities, who were attacked in many towns.

Some cities tried a new idea. In 1377, the port of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik in Croatia, made ships wait before landing. The wait was later set at 40 days. The Italian for 40 days, quaranta giorni, gave us the word *quarantine*. Today, plague is rare and can be treated with antibiotics.

words.d: the huge outbreak of plague that swept Europe, North Africa and the Middle East from 1347 to 1351
a disease caused by a bacterium usually spread by fleas; today it can be treated with antibiotics
keeping people or ships apart for a time to stop a disease from spreading

chapters.title: Looking Inside the Body
chapters.bigQuestion: What happens when people check old books against what they can see for themselves?

story.title: A Jawbone That Did Not Fit
story.kicker: A young teacher in Italy holds up a human jawbone and realizes a famous book got it wrong.
paragraphs: Padua, Italy, around 1540. Students crowd around a table in a cold lecture room. Their teacher is Andreas Vesalius, a young doctor from Brussels. Unlike many professors, he does not just read from a book while a helper does the work. He picks up the tools himself.

For more than 1,000 years, doctors had learned anatomy from Galen, a Greek physician of the 100s CE. Galen was brilliant, but in Rome he was not allowed to cut open human bodies. He studied apes, pigs and other animals instead. Most teachers assumed human bodies matched his books.

Vesalius holds a human lower jaw. Galen wrote that the lower jaw is made of two bones. In a dog, that is true. But the human jaw in Vesalius's hand is one solid bone. He checks again on other skulls. The book describes an animal, not a person.

Vesalius begins to find more places where Galen's animal studies did not fit humans. He decides to write a new book based on what he sees. In 1543 he publishes it, full of detailed pictures. Medicine starts to shift from trusting old books to checking with your own eyes.
story.think: Why might it have been hard for students to believe that Galen, their famous authority, had made mistakes?

lessons.title: The Rule of Galen
lessons.mainIdea: For over a thousand years, doctors trusted Galen's books about the body, even though he had mostly studied animals.
reading: Galen was born about 129 CE in Pergamon, in what is now Turkey. He cared for gladiators and later for Roman emperors. He wrote hundreds of works. He did clever experiments on animals, such as showing that arteries carry blood, not air.

Roman law and custom did not allow doctors to cut open human bodies for study. So Galen's *anatomy* came mostly from apes, pigs and dogs. Anatomy is the study of the body's parts and how they are arranged. Some animal parts are like ours, and some are not.

After Galen, his books became the main *authority* in medicine for Arabic, Latin and Greek readers. In medieval classrooms, a professor often read Galen aloud while an assistant cut. If the body did not match, the book usually won.

words.d: the study of the body's parts and how they are arranged
a person or book that people trust and follow as the expert

look.title: The Old Classroom
look.text: A professor sits high in a chair reading Galen in Latin. Below, an assistant cuts. A third person points at the parts. The students watch from benches. When the assistant says, "This does not look like the book," the professor keeps reading.
look.prompt: What is the problem with this way of teaching, and how would you change it?

choices: He had never seen a person

check.why: The reading says Roman law and custom did not allow human dissection.

check.q: What is anatomy?
choices: The study of the body's parts and how they are arranged
check.why: The reading defines anatomy as the study of the body's parts.

check.q: In the old classroom, what usually happened if the body did not match the book?

lessons.title: On the Fabric of the Human Body
lessons.mainIdea: In 1543, Vesalius published a detailed book of human anatomy based on what he saw himself.
reading: Andreas Vesalius was born in Brussels in 1514 and taught at the University of Padua in Italy. He did his own *dissection*, which means carefully cutting open a body to study it. He used the bodies of executed criminals, which the law then allowed.

In 1543 he published *On the Fabric of the Human Body*, often called the Fabrica. Fabric here means the structure or build of the body. It has about 700 pages and more than 200 woodcut pictures, made by skilled artists. Skeletons and muscle figures stand in landscapes, as if they are alive.

Vesalius pointed out that Galen's lower jaw, some bones and parts of the liver came from animals. He did not throw out all of Galen. He kept what matched and fixed what did not. That careful checking is why he is often called the founder of modern anatomy.

words.d: carefully cutting open a body to study its parts
the short name for Vesalius's 1543 book, On the Fabric of the Human Body

lessons.title: Pictures That Traveled
lessons.mainIdea: The printing press let accurate pictures of the body be copied exactly and shared widely.
reading: Before printing, books were copied by hand. Each copy could add small mistakes. A drawing of a muscle copied ten times might end up looking quite different from the first. Over many copies, errors piled up.

The *printing press*, developed in Europe by Johannes Gutenberg around 1450, changed this. Pictures carved in wood blocks could print the same image thousands of times. Every student could see the same accurate picture.

The Fabrica's woodcuts were copied across Europe, sometimes without permission. Doctors in many cities could now compare the same pictures with real bodies. Shared, exact pictures made it easier to spot mistakes and agree on what is true.

words.d: a machine that presses ink onto paper to make many identical copies
a picture carved into a block of wood, inked and pressed onto paper

look.prompt: What does this game show about why printing mattered for medicine?

check.why: The reading names Gutenberg as the developer of the printing press around 1450.

check.q: What problem did hand copying cause?
choices: Each copy could add small mistakes
check.why: The reading says each hand copy could add small mistakes.

check.q: How did printed pictures help doctors?
choices: They replaced the need to study bodies

check.why: Shared exact pictures made it easier to compare and spot mistakes.

lessons.title: Harvey Does the Math
lessons.mainIdea: William Harvey used measurement to show that blood must travel in a loop through the body.
reading: Galen taught that the liver made new blood from food, and the body used it up, like fuel. William Harvey, an English doctor who had studied at Padua, wondered if this could be true. He decided to measure.

Harvey estimated how much blood the heart pushes out with each beat. Then he multiplied by the number of beats. In just an hour, the total was far more blood than a person could make from food, or even more than a person's whole weight.

So, he argued, the same blood must go around and around. He called this the *circulation* of the blood. He published his work in 1628 in a book usually called On the Motion of the Heart. The *heart* is a pump, and blood makes a loop.

words.d: the movement of blood in a loop from the heart, through the body, and back
the muscle that pumps blood through the body

check.q: How did Harvey test the old idea?

check.why: The reading dates Harvey's book to 1628.

lessons.title: The Valves in the Veins
lessons.mainIdea: Simple experiments with valves in the veins showed that blood in the veins flows toward the heart.
reading: Harvey's teacher at Padua, Hieronymus Fabricius, had found small flaps inside *veins*. These flaps are called *valves*. Fabricius did not fully understand what they did. Harvey figured it out.

Harvey tied a band around a person's upper arm, so the veins below stood out. He pressed on a vein and tried to push the blood away from the heart. It would not go. Blood could only move toward the heart. The valves were one-way doors.

Anyone can see this idea in a simple test. Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins bring it back. The valves keep blood in the veins from sliding backward. Harvey's experiment used no special tools, only careful thinking and a clear test.

words.d: a blood vessel that carries blood back toward the heart
a flap that lets blood flow only one way
a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart

check.why: Veins bring blood back to the heart; arteries carry it away.

lessons.title: The Missing Link
lessons.mainIdea: Harvey could not see how blood passed from arteries to veins, but tiny vessels found later with a microscope filled the gap.
reading: Harvey's loop had a gap. Blood left the heart in arteries and came back in veins. But how did it cross from one to the other? Harvey could not see any link. He predicted there must be tiny passages too small for the eye.

In 1661, the Italian scientist Marcello Malpighi looked at a frog's lung through a *microscope*. He saw very tiny vessels joining arteries to veins. These are now called *capillaries*. They are thinner than a hair.
This shows how science often works. A good idea can make a prediction. Later, a new tool can test it. Harvey died in 1657, just before the capillaries were seen, but his prediction proved right.

words.d: a very tiny blood vessel that connects arteries and veins
a tool with lenses that makes tiny things look much bigger
a statement of what should be found if an idea is right

look.prompt: Why was Harvey's prediction useful even before anyone could see capillaries?

lessons.title: Paré and the Boiling Oil
lessons.mainIdea: When Ambroise Paré ran out of boiling oil, he found that a gentler dressing helped wounded soldiers heal better.
reading: In 1537, the French army surgeon Ambroise Paré was treating soldiers near Turin, in Italy. At the time, surgeons believed gunshot wounds were poisoned. The usual treatment was to pour boiling oil into the wound. It was very painful.

One night, Paré ran out of oil. He made a mild *dressing* instead, from egg yolk, oil of roses and turpentine. He worried all night that those soldiers would die. In the morning, they were resting with little pain and less swelling. The soldiers treated with boiling oil were in fever and pain.

Paré stopped using boiling oil. This was an accidental *comparison* between two groups. He trusted what he saw over what he had been taught. He later wrote books in French, not Latin, so that more barber-surgeons could read them.

words.d: a covering or mixture put on a wound to protect it and help it heal
looking at two groups side by side to see what is different

look.title: Two Groups of Soldiers

look.prompt: What conclusion did Paré draw, and what else would you want to know before being sure?

choices: They believed the wounds were poisoned

check.q: What happened to the soldiers who got the mild dressing?
choices: They rested with little pain and less swelling
check.why: The reading says they were resting with little pain the next morning.

check.q: Why did Paré write in French?
choices: So more barber-surgeons could read his books
check.why: The reading says he wrote in French so more barber-surgeons could read them.

lessons.title: Tying Off Blood Vessels
lessons.mainIdea: Paré used thread to tie off bleeding blood vessels during amputations instead of burning them.
reading: When a surgeon had to remove a badly hurt arm or leg, the patient could bleed to death. For centuries, surgeons stopped the bleeding with a red-hot iron. This is called *cautery*. It caused terrible pain and burns.

Paré brought back an older idea and made it common in his practice. He tied off the cut arteries with thread. A tie like this is called a *ligature*. It closed the vessel with less damage than burning. Paré also designed artificial limbs for people who had lost an arm or leg.
Paré is remembered for a humble saying about a patient's recovery: he treated the wound, and God healed it. He meant that the body does much of its own healing, and a good surgeon helps it.

words.d: burning tissue with a hot iron or chemical to stop bleeding
a thread tied around a blood vessel to close it
surgery to remove an arm, leg or other body part

lessons.title: Leeuwenhoek's Little Animals
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1670s, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used tiny homemade lenses to see living things too small for the eye.
reading: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a cloth seller in Delft, in the Netherlands. He was not trained as a scientist. But he learned to grind very small, very clear glass lenses. His simple microscopes were no bigger than a thumb.

In the 1670s he looked at pond water, rainwater and even scrapings from his own teeth. He saw tiny moving creatures. He called them *animalcules*, meaning little animals. Today we know many were single-celled living things, including *bacteria*.

Leeuwenhoek wrote long letters about what he saw to the Royal Society in London. Its members checked his claims and confirmed them. No one yet knew that some tiny living things cause disease. That link would come about 200 years later.

words.d: Leeuwenhoek's word for the tiny living creatures he saw; it means little animals
tiny single-celled living things; most are harmless or helpful, and some cause disease
a curved piece of clear glass that bends light to make things look bigger

look.title: How Much Bigger?
look.cite: Brian J. Ford, Single Lens: The Story of the Simple Microscope, 1985
look.prompt: How many times more did Leeuwenhoek's best lens magnify than a reading magnifier, roughly?

check.why: The reading says he was a cloth seller in Delft.

check.q: Where did Leeuwenhoek send his reports?
check.why: The reading says he wrote letters to the Royal Society in London.

lessons.title: See for Yourself
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1500 and 1700, doctors began to trust observation and experiment more than old authority.
reading: Look back over this chapter. Vesalius checked Galen against real bodies. Harvey measured and tested. Paré compared two groups of soldiers. Leeuwenhoek looked where no one had looked before. Each one used *observation*, careful looking, and *experiment*, a fair test.

In 1660, a group of thinkers in London formed the Royal Society. Its motto was Latin words meaning, roughly, take nobody's word for it. Claims had to be shown and checked by others. This process is part of what we now call the *scientific method*.

Old books were not useless. Galen and Ibn Sina had gathered a lot of real knowledge. But the new rule was that any idea, however famous, could be tested. When the test disagreed with the book, the test should win.

words.d: careful looking and noting what you see
a fair test designed to find out whether an idea is right
a way of learning by asking questions, testing ideas and checking results with others
